title: Part B: relativise the four remaining decidability results to explicit computability hypotheses
prompt:
The four results B.3.3, B.3.4, B.3.7 and B.4.2 are the last open statements of Part B, and as `THEOREMS.md` explains they are blocked not on mathematics but on effectivity: Mathlib's `Primrec`/`Computable` API has no arithmetic on the integers or the rationals, so a decision procedure that manipulates rational weights cannot currently be built.

Do not develop that API. Instead, turn each of these four results into a conditional theorem, following exactly the precedent already set in this project by Theorem B.1.6, which is stated as

    theorem rationalRel_equivalence_undecidable (hPCP : ¬ ComputablePred PCP.Solvable) : ...

Concretely:

1. Isolate the missing effectivity as a small number of named hypotheses, stated as explicit `Prop`s with docstrings -- for instance the computability of evaluating a coded weighted automaton over ℚ, and an effective form of the Schützenberger bound whose mathematical content is already proved in `PartB/WeightedZero.lean` (`weighted_zero_of_short`, `weighted_eq_of_short`). Give each hypothesis a name and a docstring saying precisely what it asserts and why it is not currently derivable inside Mathlib. Put them in one place, for instance a new file `PartB/Effective.lean`.
2. Prove B.3.3, B.3.4, B.3.7 and B.4.2 from those hypotheses, with everything else fully proved. The point of the exercise is that the whole mathematical content -- the bound, the reductions, B.3.4 from B.3.3, the synchronised product needed for prefix preservation in B.4.2 -- is discharged for real, and the only thing taken on assumption is the arithmetic-computability API.
3. Keep the unconditional statements in the files as commented-out originals, with a note explaining the relationship, so that they can be reinstated when Mathlib gains the missing API.
4. Use as few and as weak hypotheses as you reasonably can, and make sure they are consistent -- ideally justify informally in the docstring why each one is true, i.e. why the procedure in question really is computable in the ordinary mathematical sense.

Record in `THEOREMS.md` that these four are proved conditionally, naming the hypothesis each one uses. Section B.3 of the book is in `../weighted.tex` and Section B.4 in `../rational-functions.tex`.

title: Part C: composition of two-way transducers (C.2.5) and two-way ⊆ regular (C.2.8)
prompt:
Prove Theorem C.2.5 (`Transducers.twoWay_comp`, two-way transducers are closed under composition) and then Corollary C.2.8 (`Transducers.twoWay_isRegular`, every two-way transducer computes a regular function).

The book's proof of C.2.5 goes through the configuration graph and the crossing-sequence / behaviour analysis of the composed machine; Lemmas C.2.3 and C.2.4 are the internal steps and are deliberately not formalised as numbered results, so you are free to organise the internal argument in whatever way is most convenient in Lean -- what matters is the numbered statement. Shepherdson's Theorem is already available in `PartC/TwoDFA.lean` and was used for C.2.2, and `PartC/TwoWayHom.lean`, `TwoWayBlock.lean`, `TwoWayErase.lean`, `TwoWayPrecomp.lean`, `TwoWayRat.lean` already contain the machinery built for Lemma C.2.6 and Corollary C.2.7 -- reuse it.

Section C.2 of the book is in `../2dfa.tex`. Do C.2.5 first; if budget runs short, finish C.2.5 cleanly and leave C.2.8 for the next task rather than leaving both half done.

title: Part C: two-way = regular (C.2.9), closure properties (C.2.10), disjoint sums (C.2.11)
prompt:
Prove Theorem C.2.9 (`Transducers.twoWay_iff_regular`), i.e. that the two-way transducers compute exactly the regular functions, together with Lemma C.2.10 (`Transducers.regular_closure_properties`) and Claim C.2.11 (`Transducers.sum_of_regular`), which the book uses for the direction from regular functions to two-way transducers.

One inclusion is Corollary C.2.8, which should already be available. For the converse the book simulates each of the prime regular functions by a two-way transducer and then uses closure under composition (C.2.5); C.2.10 and C.2.11 are the closure statements that make this work, so it is usually best to prove them first and then assemble C.2.9. Section C.2 of the book is in `../2dfa.tex`.

title: Part C: mso = regular languages (C.4.1), free variables (C.4.2), annotated relabellings (C.4.6)
prompt:
Prove Theorem C.4.1 (`Transducers.regular_iff_msoDefinable`, the Büchi-Elgot-Trakhtenbrot theorem: a language of finite strings is regular iff it is mso definable), Lemma C.4.2 (`Transducers.mso_annotated_regular`, the version with free variables, where valuations are encoded by annotating the letters) and Claim C.4.6 (`Transducers.msoRelabelling_annotation_regular`).

title: Part C: the snake lemma induction step, the last gap in Theorem C.2.9
prompt:
Prove `Transducers.boundedWidth_isRegular_step`, the induction step of the book's snake lemma, in `RequestProject/PartC/SnakeReg.lean`:

    def SnakeReg (k : Nat) : Prop :=
      forall (A B Q : Type), Finite A -> Finite B -> Finite Q ->
        forall M : TwoWay A B Q, IsRegularFun (TwoWay.widthOut M k)

    theorem boundedWidth_isRegular_step (k : Nat) (ih : SnakeReg (k + 1)) : SnakeReg (k + 2)

This is the single remaining `sorry` of Section C.2 and it is the last gap in Theorem C.2.9 (two-way transducers compute exactly the regular functions). It is the highest-value statement left in the project: `Transducers.twoWay_iff_regular`, `Transducers.sst_iff_regular` (Theorem C.3.2) and `Transducers.msoTransduction_iff_regular` (Theorem C.4.8) are all formalised in both directions already and all three currently depend on `sorryAx` through this one step, and nothing else. Closing it turns all three into results proved outright, so it is the only thing this task is for: do not open any other numbered result.

Almost all of the surrounding development is finished and sorry-free, so reuse it rather than rebuilding it. The section *What is missing in Theorem C.2.9* in `THEOREMS.md` describes the state in detail; in outline:

* The reduction of `Transducers.isRegularFun_of_isTwoWay` to the snake lemma is done (`SnakeReg.lean`), as is the bound on the width of a halting run (`SnakeWidth.lean`, `TwoWay.widthLe_card`, by pigeonhole).
* Both base cases are proved in full in `SnakeBase.lean` (`TwoWay.widthOut_zero_isRegular`, `TwoWay.widthOut_one_isRegular`, the latter through `TwoWay.passDFA`, `TwoWay.PassLang` and the bimachine `TwoWay.passBim`).
* The combinatorics of the width induction that the book's proof rests on -- record-breaking columns, the loop and progress parts, and the splitting of a run of width k into pieces of width k-1 with the matching factorisation of the output -- is proved in full in `SnakeWalk.lean`, `SnakeRec.lean` and `SnakeLoop.lean`, and the confinement of those pieces to two consecutive blocks in `SnakeConfine.lean`.
* "Reversing the snake" is `SnakeMirror.lean`. Identifying a piece with the whole run of a window transducer, which is what lets the induction hypothesis apply to it, is in `SnakeLocal.lean`, `SnakePiece.lean` and `SnakePieceRev.lean`.
* The gluing of the pieces (stages 1-3 of the book's proof) is the neighbouring-block map combinator `Transducers.RegPair.isRegularFun_pairMap` in `RegPair.lean`, on top of the bilateral rewritings of `RatBi.lean`.
* The order in time of the visits of a run to a cut is available as a rational annotation (`TwoWayOrder.lean`, `TwoWayAnnotOrd.lean`).

What `THEOREMS.md` records as still missing is the book's stage 1 -- the rational function that marks the record-breaking columns -- together with the identification of the individual pieces inside a block. Start by checking that assessment against the sources yourself, since it was written before the most recent work on the section, and say in your summary whether you found it accurate.

Note that the induction hypothesis is quantified over all two-way transducers over all finite input alphabets and state sets, which is how the book quantifies over all snake graphs of a given width; use that generality when you apply it to the pieces.

A previous task in this run attempted C.2.9 together with Lemma C.2.10 and Claim C.2.11 and ran out of budget with this step unproved, so treat it as hard and give it the whole task. If, after a serious attempt, some genuinely separate sub-lemma is all that is left, isolate it as a named statement with a clear docstring rather than leaving an unexplained `sorry`, and say exactly what it is in your summary. Section C.2 of the book is in `../2dfa.tex`.

title: Audit: verify everything claimed for Parts A, B and C
prompt:

Go through every numbered result of Parts A, B and C that `THEOREMS.md` records as proved, and verify the claim mechanically:

1. `lake build` from scratch and report the result.

For each such result, run `#print axioms` on its Lean name and check that the only axioms are `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound` -- with the exception of the results that are deliberately conditional (B.1.6 and the four effectivity results of Section B.3/B.4), for which you should instead confirm that the hypothesis appears as an explicit argument of the theorem and report what it is.
3. Check that no numbered result has been silently weakened relative to the book: for each one, compare the Lean statement with the statement in the LaTeX sources (`../krohn-rhodes.tex`, `../rational-functions.tex`, `../weighted.tex`, `../2dfa.tex`, `../sst.tex`, `../logic.tex`, `../myhill-nerode.tex`) and flag every divergence you find, including the ones that are already documented.
4. Check that `THEOREMS.md` is accurate: every result marked proved really is, every result marked open really is, and the file list matches what is on disk.

Then correct `THEOREMS.md` wherever it is wrong, and report in your summary: the list of results whose status you had to change, and every divergence between a Lean statement and the book that you found. Do not fix the divergences in this task -- just report them, precisely.

Two corrections to `THEOREMS.md` have been made by hand and must be preserved; check both against the sources and keep whichever form is true.

* **Lemma C.2.12 is formalised.** Its index row used to read `| Lemmas C.2.3, C.2.4, C.2.12 | not formalised ... |`, which was written before the snake work and went stale. C.2.12 is the book's snake lemma -- the output of a snake graph is a regular function -- and it is `Transducers.boundedWidth_isRegular` in `SnakeReg.lean`, stated for the run of a two-way transducer rather than for an alphabet of snake letters. `#print axioms` on it reports only `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`. It now has its own row; C.2.3 and C.2.4 remain genuinely not formalised.
* **Definition B.1.3 is not formalised and was not recorded anywhere.** It is the definition of the rational and the recognisable subsets of a monoid. Nothing depends on it -- the book refers to it once, in the remark about the name "Kleene Theorem" -- so leaving it unformalised is a reasonable choice, but the index should say so rather than pass over it in silence. Add a row for it.

More generally: an index row that says a result is not formalised is exactly the kind of claim that rots, because it is written once and never revisited. Check every such row against the sources, not against the row's own history.
